c.tagline: Ancient walled city rising again after years of war.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rarely used in practice; agree on the fare with the driver before departing, or have your hotel arrange the ride.

emergency.note: Dispatchers may not speak English; ask hotel staff to help contact emergency services.

avoid.reason: Avoid former front-line suburbs such as Jobar, Yarmouk and parts of Eastern Ghouta, where war damage, unexploded ordnance and checkpoints remain.
Never photograph checkpoints, soldiers or government buildings, carry ID at all times, and expect frequent security checks moving around the city.

hood_desc: UNESCO-listed walled Old City with Roman-era gates, the Umayyad Mosque and winding stone lanes lined with courtyard houses turned boutique hotels, cafes and bars; best for culture-focused travelers who want to be inside the historic core, though rooms are small and utilities can be inconsistent.

Leafy, upscale diplomatic quarter with embassies, UN offices and international restaurants just west of the Old City; the most reliable power, water and security in the city, favored by business travelers, NGO staff and anyone wanting international-standard comfort.

The bustling commercial heart between the Old City and Umayyad Square, packed with shops, street food stalls and the famed covered Hamidiyeh Souq; convenient and walkable but noisier, suited to budget-to-midrange travelers who want to be in the thick of city life.

A quieter Ottoman-era quarter just outside the old walls near the Bahsa transport hub, known for cheap guesthouses and an unpolished, local feel; popular with backpackers and long-stay budget travelers.

Modern, quiet residential district southwest of downtown housing embassies, NGOs and newer hotels with dependable infrastructure; best for travelers who prioritize calm and reliability over proximity to the sights.

water.note: Avoid tap water given damaged infrastructure; use bottled water.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash (Syrian pounds) directly to the driver or a conductor; there is no citywide smart card or app-based payment system. Fares are very low, typically well under a dollar.
transit.hours: Roughly 6:00-22:00 for most bus and microbus routes; taxis fill in for night travel.
transit.note: No metro or tram; the city relies on buses and shared microbuses, supplemented heavily by taxis.

train: Chemins de Fer Syriens (CFS) domestic rail - service limited/suspended on many lines due to war damage

airport.name: Damascus International Airport (DAM)
airport.drive: 30-45 min (25 km southeast of city center; longer at checkpoints)
rentals: Local agencies at arrivals hall (no major international chains currently operating due to sanctions)

transit.m: Public bus/microbus to Baramkeh station (~45-60 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or about 10% in restaurants and hotels is appreciated, and small tips for porters and drivers are customary.
